name: Furtive fallacy
statement: Treating hidden malign agency as the standing explanation of events, so that the facts that matter are assumed to be the dark and dirty ones.
meaning: Fischer's definition is that this is "the erroneous idea that facts of special significance are dark and dirty things and that history itself is a story of causes mostly insidious and results mostly invidious". It begins, he writes, with the premise "that reality is a sordid, secret thing", and it combines "a naive epistemological assumption that things are never what they seem to be, with a firm attachment to the doctrine of original sin". The distinction he draws next is the one his retellings drop. The fallacy is "something more, and something other than merely a conspiracy theory, though that form of causal reduction is a common component". What is fallacious is the standing assumption rather than any particular allegation, so a historian who concludes from evidence that a given plot happened has not committed it. Fischer files the error under fallacies of factual significance, which are errors about which facts matter, and not under fallacies of causation. This is a charge about a piece of writing rather than a measurement of a mind. Its measured neighbour is conspiracy mentality, the disposition psychologists assess with generic questionnaire items about hidden actors. Finding structure in noise belongs to apophenia and attributing a purposeful actor to agent detection, and both have their own entries.

origin.where: Historians' Fallacies: Toward a Logic of Historical Thought
origin.note: Fischer's book is where the name entered use. The section runs from page 74 to page 78 of chapter III, "Fallacies of Factual Significance", and the index of fallacies lists the entry at 74-8 and 210. The copyright page reads 1970. Fischer was not the first into print with the phrase. An unsigned review of Sabine Baring-Gould's The Tragedy of the Caesars uses the phrase 77 years earlier. It is article III of the Edinburgh Review for July 1893, pages 55 to 82. On page 79 the reviewer writes that "it is easy, when this furtive fallacy has tacitly been adopted, to show modern readers" that no adequate motive can be assigned for the atrocities history charges to Nero and his mother. The strings "Baring" and "Edinburgh" do not occur in Fischer's text, which was searched in full.

evidence:
The book argues by specimen and contains no experiment, no sample and no rate in these five pages. Fischer's targets are American historians of the Constitution. Algie Simons is quoted writing that "the organic law of this nation was formulated in secret session by a body called into existence through a conspiratory [sic] trick". Charles Beard supplies the central case twice over. The first is An Economic Interpretation of the Constitution, of 1913. The second is Beard's 1948 book on American entry into the Second World War, whose thesis Fischer summarises as Roosevelt and his cronies secretly manipulating policy "by a series of subtle and sordid tricks". Fischer calls the 1913 book "a very moderate specimen" and writes that "no imputation of paranoia can attach to his work". Forrest McDonald's E Pluribus Unum supplies the gross case, a secret 1787 deal in a smoke-filled room that Fischer says has no evidence behind it and that he wondered was "intended as a practical joke". A fifth specimen runs the other way. Joseph Hamburger reads the philosophic radicals' threat of revolution as a calculated bluff. Fischer calls that an inversion of the fallacy, grounded in the assumption that reality is less than meets the eye. He takes the wider diagnosis from Richard Hofstadter on the muckrakers of the Progressive era, for whom reality "was hidden, neglected, and off-stage".

The disposition Fischer describes has since been measured, by a different discipline and under a different name. Bruder, Haffke, Neave, Nouripanah and Imhoff built the five-item Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire around generic statements. One reads "I think that events which superficially seem to lack a connection are often the result of secret activities". Another reads "I think that there are secret organizations that greatly influence political decisions". In a cross-cultural sample of 7,766 the scale came out one-dimensional. Alpha was 0.84 in German, 0.84 in English and 0.72 in Turkish. It correlated with each of 33 specific conspiracy items at between 0.37 and 0.76, averaging 0.58. Imhoff and Bruder had earlier argued that the disposition is best read as a generalised political attitude, distinct from right-wing authoritarianism and social dominance orientation, and related to prejudice against high-power groups rather than low-power ones. The two meta-analyses report correlations of modest size. Bowes, Costello and Tasimi synthesised 170 studies, 257 samples, 52 variables, 1,429 effect sizes and 158,473 participants, and put the strongest correlates at perceiving danger and threat, relying on intuition and holding odd beliefs, and being antagonistic and acting superior. Biddlestone, Green, Douglas, Azevedo, Sutton and Cichocka analysed 971 effect sizes from 279 studies and 137,406 participants. Epistemic motives came out at k = 114, r = .14, existential at k = 121, r = .16, and social at k = 100, r = .16. They report considerable heterogeneity throughout, and weaker relationships in experiments than in correlational designs.

replication.headline: No study was found that measures the furtive fallacy in historians or in anyone else. The nearest measured thing is conspiracy mentality, where the questionnaire travels well and several of the psychological explanations attached to it do not.
replication.detail:
Europe PMC holds no record containing the phrase "furtive fallacy". Crossref returns nothing under it either; its bibliographic search degrades to loose matching and offers an Oxford English Dictionary entry for the adjective and a Lancet piece called "Furtive expedients". Nothing located turns Fischer's charge into a rate, and no study was found that scores historical writing for the error.

What has been repeated is the measurement of the disposition. Ćirović and Pedović tested the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire in Serbian, Bulgarian, Greek and English across 2,897 participants. Metric invariance held across languages and scalar invariance across genders. Scalar invariance across education held for three of the four samples and not for the English one. Imhoff, Zimmer, Klein and 38 co-authors ran the scale across 26 countries. The generic measure correlated with an aggregate of agreement with concrete conspiracy theories at r = .49, 95% CI [.41, .56], rising to .73 after correction for attenuation.

The explanations attached to the disposition have fared less well than the measure. In the same 26-country work, the claim that conspiracy mentality is stronger on the political right held in Study 1, B = 0.115, SE = 0.037, p = .005, 95% CI [0.042, 0.187]. Study 2 did not reproduce it, B = 0.068, SE = 0.072, p = .362, with an interval running from -0.073 to 0.210. The curvilinear claim, greater conspiracy mentality at both extremes, held in both studies, B = 0.062, SE = 0.017, p = .001 and B = 0.220, SE = 0.031, p < .001. The authors report large heterogeneity across countries in the linear relation, with the effect running leftward in Hungary, Romania and Spain. Dieguez, Wagner-Egger and Gauvrit tested the "nothing happens by accident" reading of the fallacy directly, in three studies. They report failing to find the predicted association between a low prior for randomness and conspiracist ideation, even when randomness was set explicitly against malevolent human intervention. That paper and its later replication are handled on this site's apophenia entry rather than repeated here. Van Prooijen, Wahring, Mausolf, Mulas and Shwan reopened the best-known result in the field, that beliefs in contradictory conspiracy theories correlate positively. Across four preregistered studies and 7,641 adults evaluating 28 contradictory pairs, the positive correlation replicated every time. It was mostly produced by participants who believed the official account of the event. Among those who disbelieved the official account the correlation was inconsistent, and a mini meta-analysis of that subgroup returned a negative correlation.

limits:
No effect sizes appear in the structured fields. The entry's own subject is a charge about historical prose and has no effect size, and pairing a meta-analytic correlation from the conspiracy literature with it would invent a comparison no source makes.

Several numbers in the sources disagree with each other and are reported here as they stand. Bruder and colleagues give their retest sample as N = 141 in the abstract and as 133 of 177 in the method. The method is where the retest correlation of 0.84 over a 15-day gap is printed, and its figure is the one used above. Imhoff and colleagues give a combined N of 104,253 in both the published abstract and the accepted manuscript. The manuscript's introduction gives Study 1 as 33,431. Its methods and figure captions give Study 1 as 37,692 and Study 2 as 70,882, which sum to 108,574. The country count of 26 and the combined 104,253 were confirmed against the published abstract at the publisher.

Several documents could not be read. Wikipedia names Jeffrey Bale's article on bogus conspiracy theories against genuine conspiratorial politics as the standing criticism of Fischer's idea. It is closed at the publisher, has no copy recorded by Unpaywall, has its abstract elided at Semantic Scholar, and returned a bot check at the journal site. Only its title, authorship, journal and page range of 45 to 60 were verified, at Crossref. Dieguez, Wagner-Egger and Gauvrit is paywalled with no open copy recorded, so it is quoted here only from its PubMed abstract and no sample sizes from it appear. Both meta-analyses are behind the American Psychological Association and are quoted from their abstracts, read at PubMed and again at Europe PMC; no per-variable correlation from Bowes and colleagues is given, because the abstract prints none. Imhoff and colleagues was read as the author accepted manuscript deposited at HAL, not as the published article, and the two downloads had the same checksum, so the figures rest on one file rather than two independent renderings.

The search for a measurement of the fallacy itself covered Europe PMC by phrase, Crossref by bibliographic query and general web search. No psychology-specific database such as PsycINFO was searched and OpenAlex was not queried. Fischer's text was read as two independent renderings of the same Internet Archive scan, a PDF and the plain-text rendering, and every quotation above was checked in both. The 1893 Edinburgh Review passage was likewise read in the item's plain text and again in an extraction from its PDF. Neither Baring-Gould's book nor Hofstadter's Age of Reform was obtained, and the Hofstadter and Simons wording here comes from Fischer's quotations of them.
misreadings:
The commonest error is to treat the fallacy as a synonym for believing in conspiracy theories. Fischer's own sentence rules that out: the fallacy is "something more, and something other than merely a conspiracy theory". His charge is against a standing assumption about how history happens, and the specimens he picks are professional historians rather than pamphleteers. Nothing in the section says that conspiracies do not occur. Elsewhere in the book Fischer lists Bernard Bailyn's hypothesis, that Americans went to war against England partly because they feared a deliberate conspiracy against their freedom, among the explanatory hypotheses that are not tautologies, adding that all of them may be right or wrong. What the section does not supply, in the five pages read here in full, is a test for telling a warranted conspiracy explanation from the fallacy, and that gap is where Fischer's critics have gone.

The empirical literature has had to solve the same problem, and it solves it by refusing to grade the beliefs. Nera and Schöpfer propose defining conspiracy theories as claims that the public is being pervasively lied to about some aspect of reality, and say plainly that the definition "does not take position regarding the truth value of conspiracy theories". The questionnaires follow suit. One of the five Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire items reads "I think that government agencies closely monitor all citizens". It was the lowest-endorsed item in all three languages at publication in April 2013, at 3.35 in German and 3.90 in English on an eleven-point scale. A preprint illustrates the position rather than settling it. In two Prolific samples of 331 and 412 American residents, conspiracy mentality correlated positively with belief in warranted conspiracies as well as unwarranted ones, more strongly with the unwarranted. Its authors read that as evidence that a high conspiracy mentality carries some value.

A second error is to read Fischer as diagnosing paranoia. He writes that in an extreme form the fallacy is "not merely an intellectual error but a mental illness which is commonly called paranoia". A footnote to that sentence adds "of course, I do not mean to suggest that the historians whose works are used as examples of this error are paranoid". Alsuhibani, Shevlin, Freeman, Sheaves and Bentall put the question to data in three samples of 496, 1,519 and 638. A two-correlated-factor model of paranoia and conspiracy belief fitted better than a single factor in every one. Paranoia was tied to negative self-esteem, and conspiracy belief to positive self-esteem in the two larger samples.

A third is to take Fischer's alarm about his own moment as a finding. He wrote that "nothing is more ominous in our own time than the prevalence of furtive fallacies in every ideological camp". His examples include Macbird, the campaign against Axel Springer, and fears of furtive acts by soldiers, students, Communists, capitalists and the Mafia. Uscinski and colleagues tested the modern form of that claim across four studies, seven nations and comparisons spanning between seven months and 55 years. Beliefs in 13 of 52 conspiracy theories rose over time, and decreases outnumbered increases and were larger. In the European study only one of 35 comparisons rose, Holocaust denial in Sweden from 1% to 3%, p = 0.016, against seven significant decreases and 27 cases of no change.

A fourth is Wikipedia's account of the earlier printing. Its article reports that the phrase appeared in an anonymous 1893 critique of Baring-Gould and that "the usage was, then, inverted from Fischer's: Baring-Gould argued that well-attested scoundrels were secretly benign". The sentence carrying the phrase says something narrower. The reviewer has just written that Baring-Gould "seems to draw his standard of motives through the moral medium of the modern world", and it is that tacitly adopted anachronism which the phrase names. In 1893 the furtive thing is the assumption, not the agency, which is closer to what Fischer files 70 pages later as presentism than to the error he gave the name to.

sources.text: Fischer, D. H. (1970). Historians' Fallacies: Toward a Logic of Historical Thought. New York: Harper & Row. Pages 74 to 78 read in full for the definition, the conspiracy-theory distinction, the Perry, Hofstadter, Simons, Beard, McDonald and Hamburger specimens and footnote 27; page 34 for the Bailyn hypothesis; pages 209 to 213 for the index's second locator. Read as the Internet Archive scan, both the PDF and the plain-text rendering of the same item, and every quotation checked in both.

Anon. (1893). The Tragedy of the Caesars: A Study of the Characters of the Caesars of the Julian and Claudian Houses. By S. Baring Gould. The Edinburgh Review, or Critical Journal, volume 178, number 365, July 1893, pages 55 to 82. The phrase "this furtive fallacy" appears on page 79. Read as the Internet Archive item's plain text and again in an extraction from its PDF.

Bruder, M., Haffke, P., Neave, N., Nouripanah, N., & Imhoff, R. (2013). Measuring individual differences in generic beliefs in conspiracy theories across cultures: Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, 225. Full text read at Europe PMC. Source for the five items, the alphas, the sample of 7,766, the retest figures and the correlations with 33 specific conspiracy items.

Imhoff, R., & Bruder, M. (2014). Speaking (un-)truth to power: Conspiracy mentality as a generalised political attitude. European Journal of Personality, 28(1), 25-43. Abstract read at Crossref; the full text was not obtained.

Imhoff, R., Zimmer, F., Klein, O., et al. (2022). Conspiracy mentality and political orientation across 26 countries. Nature Human Behaviour, 6(3), 392-403. Figures read from the author accepted manuscript deposited at HAL. The 26 countries and the combined N of 104,253 were confirmed separately against the published abstract at nature.com.

Ćirović, N., & Pedović, I. (2025). Construct validity, measurement invariance, and nomological network of Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (CMQ) across four different languages. Journal of Personality Assessment, 107(5), 658-670. Abstract read at PubMed; the full text was not obtained.

Bowes, S. M., Costello, T. H., & Tasimi, A. (2023). The conspiratorial mind: A meta-analytic review of motivational and personological correlates. Psychological Bulletin, 149(5-6), 259-293. Abstract read at PubMed and again at Europe PMC; the full text is behind the publisher and was not obtained.

Biddlestone, M., Green, R., Douglas, K. M., Azevedo, F., Sutton, R. M., & Cichocka, A. (2025). Reasons to believe: A systematic review and meta-analytic synthesis of the motives associated with conspiracy beliefs. Psychological Bulletin, 151(1), 48-87. Abstract read at PubMed and again at Europe PMC; the full text is behind the publisher and was not obtained.

van Prooijen, J.-W., Wahring, I., Mausolf, L., Mulas, N., & Shwan, S. (2023). Just dead, not alive: Reconsidering belief in contradictory conspiracy theories. Psychological Science, 34(6), 670-682. Abstract read at PubMed and again at Europe PMC; the full text was not obtained.

Dieguez, S., Wagner-Egger, P., & Gauvrit, N. (2015). Nothing happens by accident, or does it? A low prior for randomness does not explain belief in conspiracy theories. Psychological Science, 26(11), 1762-1770. Paywalled with no open copy recorded by Unpaywall; quoted here only from the PubMed abstract. Its numbers are handled on this site's apophenia entry.

Uscinski, J., Enders, A. M., Klofstad, C., et al. (2022). Have beliefs in conspiracy theories increased over time? PLOS ONE, 17(7), e0270429. Full text read at Europe PMC. Source for the 52 conspiracy theories, the 35 European comparisons and the Swedish figure.

Alsuhibani, A., Shevlin, M., Freeman, D., Sheaves, B., & Bentall, R. P. (2022). Why conspiracy theorists are not always paranoid: Conspiracy theories and paranoia form separate factors with distinct psychological predictors. PLOS ONE, 17(4), e0259053. Abstract read at PubMed and again at Europe PMC; the full text was not obtained.

Nera, K., & Schöpfer, C. (2023). What is so special about conspiracy theories? Conceptually distinguishing beliefs in conspiracy theories from conspiracy beliefs in psychological research. Theory & Psychology, 33(2), 287-305. Abstract read at Crossref from the authors' preprint record, which carries the wording quoted here; the journal version was not obtained.

When belief in warranted conspiracy theories is warranted: Conspiracy mentality and belief in warranted and unwarranted conspiracy theories. PsyArXiv preprint, version 3, 2026. Not peer reviewed. Abstract read at Europe PMC; the full text was not obtained, and the sample sizes of 331 and 412 come from that abstract.

Bale, J. M. (2007). Political paranoia v. political realism: on distinguishing between bogus conspiracy theories and genuine conspiratorial politics. Patterns of Prejudice, 41(1), 45-60. Title, authorship, journal and page range verified at Crossref. The article is closed, has no copy recorded by Unpaywall, has its abstract elided at Semantic Scholar, and the publisher page returned a bot check, so it was not read.
Wikipedia, Furtive fallacy. Used to find sources and quoted here as the carrier of the claim about the 1893 usage being an inversion of Fischer's, not relied on for anything else.
